studyMetadata.subtitle: Part I: Created but Fallen
studyMetadata.description: Who are we, and how did we come to be this way? This study accompanies Part I of Made, Marred and Renewed (Volume 1 of Rick Creighton’s Doctrine for Disciple-Making), a theology textbook for church leaders, students and thoughtful lay people. Each session takes about an hour and works through the key Bible passages behind one chapter, with questions you can answer from the text itself. Use it with a group or on your own; the chapter is built in, to read afterwards if you wish.

elements.text:
Daniel’s wife died eight months ago after a short illness. He still comes to church every week, sits in the same place, and sings the songs – but something in him has gone quiet. ‘I believe in the resurrection,’ he tells his pastor. ‘I just don’t feel that it changes anything. She’s still gone. The house is still empty. I can’t see how any of that is going to be undone.’

Whether he realises it or not, Daniel is facing a question of theology: how what he believes connects with how he lives and grieves – the subject of this chapter.

Daniel is a composite character, not a real individual.

elements.question: What do you think is really going on for Daniel? If you were his friend, what would you want to say to him – and what would you avoid saying?

elements.text: Some people picture theology like a brick wall: each belief rests on the ones below it, so one crack threatens the whole thing. Others picture it like a spider’s web: many strands, connected in all directions, which can bend and still hold. Look at the two pictures below, then answer honestly.

elements.question: Look at the two pictures. Which is closer to how your own beliefs fit together? If one belief were shaken, what else would feel at risk?

elements.text: 1. Waking up to what we already believe

elements.passageText:
8For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Live as children of light 9(for the fruit of the light consists in all goodness, righteousness and truth) 10and find out what pleases the Lord. 11Have nothing to do with the fruitless deeds of darkness, but rather expose them. 12It is shameful even to mention what the disobedient do in secret. 13But everything exposed by the light becomes visible – and everything that is illuminated becomes a light. 14This is why it is said:

‘Wake up, sleeper,
rise from the dead,
and Christ will shine on you.’

elements.question: Paul quotes a wake-up call in verse 14. Who is being addressed, and what is promised? Those who wake are not starting from nothing: verses 8–11 describe the life they were already living and the life they now live. What does the light do to what was already there (vv11–13), and what are they to discover (v10)?
elements.questionHint: Look at what the readers once were (v8) and what the light does to things already around them (v13).
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul addresses a sleeper, someone as good as dead, and promises that Christ will shine on them. Those who wake are not starting from nothing: they already had a way of living, which Paul calls darkness (vv8–11). The light exposes what was already there and makes it visible (vv11–13), and the person who is awake is to discover what pleases the Lord (v10). In the same way, we wake up in the middle of a life, and a theology, that is already being lived, and now have the chance to look at it honestly.

elements.question: Do you need a degree to do theology? Think about it before tapping ‘Find out’.
elements.answer: No. Everybody is some sort of theologian, whether or not they have ever studied. We all have some answer to the big questions: Is there a God? What is he like? What happens at death? The real question is not whether we have a theology, but whether we reflect on the theology we already have, and whether we are growing in it.

elements.passageText: 24‘Therefore everyone who hears these words of mine and puts them into practice is like a wise man who built his house on the rock. 25The rain came down, the streams rose, and the winds blew and beat against that house; yet it did not fall, because it had its foundation on the rock. 26But everyone who hears these words of mine and does not put them into practice is like a foolish man who built his house on sand. 27The rain came down, the streams rose, and the winds blew and beat against that house, and it fell with a great crash.’

elements.question: Both builders hear Jesus’ words. What is the only difference between them, and what do the rain, floods and wind reveal?
elements.sampleAnswer: Both men hear Jesus’ words; the only difference is that the wise man puts them into practice and the foolish man does not. The rain, streams and wind come against both houses in the same way. They reveal what each house was built on. Hearing without doing is like building on sand: it stands only until the storm comes.

elements.passageText:
1Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ to further the faith of God’s elect and their knowledge of the truth that leads to godliness – 2in the hope of eternal life, which God, who does not lie, promised before the beginning of time, 3and which now at his appointed season he has brought to light through the preaching entrusted to me by the command of God our Saviour,

…

11For the grace of God has appeared that offers salvation to all people. 12It teaches us to say ‘No’ to ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright and godly lives in this present age, 13while we wait for the blessed hope – the appearing of the glory of our great God and Saviour, Jesus Christ, 14who gave himself for us to redeem us from all wickedness and to purify for himself a people that are his very own, eager to do what is good.

elements.question: Put the two passages together. What is the ‘knowledge of the truth’ meant to lead to (1:1)? What does God’s grace ‘teach’ us (2:12), what are we waiting for (2:13), and why did Jesus give himself (2:14)?
elements.questionHint: Look for the repeated link between truth, grace and the way we live.
elements.sampleAnswer: The knowledge of the truth is meant to lead to godliness (1:1). God’s grace teaches us to say no to ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright and godly lives in the present age (2:12). Meanwhile we wait for the appearing of the glory of our great God and Saviour, Jesus Christ (2:13). He gave himself to redeem us from all wickedness and to purify a people who are eager to do what is good (2:14). Truth and grace are both aimed at changed lives.

elements.passageText:
3For what I received I passed on to you as of first importance: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, 4that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures,

…

12But if it is preached that Christ has been raised from the dead, how can some of you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? 13If there is no resurrection of the dead, then not even Christ has been raised. 14And if Christ has not been raised, our preaching is useless and so is your faith. 15More than that, we are then found to be false witnesses about God, for we have testified about God that he raised Christ from the dead. But he did not raise him if in fact the dead are not raised. 16For if the dead are not raised, then Christ has not been raised either. 17And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile; you are still in your sins. 18Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ are lost. 19If only for this life we have hope in Christ, we are of all people most to be pitied.

elements.question: Paul says the gospel he received is ‘of first importance’ (vv3–4). Reading verses 12–19, list what Paul says would be lost if Christ had not been raised.
elements.sampleAnswer: If Christ has not been raised, Paul’s preaching is useless and so is the faith of those who believe it (v14). The apostles would be false witnesses, because they testified that God raised Christ (v15). Faith would be futile and we would still be in our sins (v17). Those who have died in Christ would be lost (v18), and Christians would be the most to be pitied of all people (v19).

elements.passageText:
20But Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. 21For since death came through a man, the resurrection of the dead comes also through a man. 22For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive.

…

42So will it be with the resurrection of the dead. The body that is sown is perishable, it is raised imperishable; 43it is sown in dishonour, it is raised in glory; it is sown in weakness, it is raised in power; 44it is sown a natural body, it is raised a spiritual body.

If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual body. 45So it is written: ‘The first man Adam became a living being’; the last Adam, a life-giving spirit. 46The spiritual did not come first, but the natural, and after that the spiritual. 47The first man was of the dust of the earth; the second man is of heaven. 48As was the earthly man, so are those who are of the earth; and as is the heavenly man, so also are those who are of heaven. 49And just as we have borne the image of the earthly man, so shall we bear the image of the heavenly man.

elements.question: Paul contrasts Adam and Christ (vv20–22, 45). What does each bring, and to whom? What kind of body does Paul say believers will receive (vv42–44, 49)?
elements.questionHint: Look at the pairs: death and life, perishable and imperishable, natural and spiritual.
elements.sampleAnswer: In Adam all die; in Christ all will be made alive (v22). Christ is the firstfruits of those who have died (v20), the beginning of a harvest still to come. The body is sown perishable and natural, and raised imperishable and spiritual (vv42–44). Just as we have borne the image of the earthly man, we will also bear the image of the heavenly man (v49). The raised body is real but transformed.

elements.question: Paul says ‘in Adam’ all die and ‘in Christ’ all will be made alive. How can one person’s action affect so many others? Think of an example, then tap ‘Find out’.
elements.answer: The word has two senses. Symbolic representation is like a flag standing for a country: it does nothing. Active representation is different: when a national team goes to the World Cup, or a president signs a treaty at the UN, they act on behalf of everyone they represent. If the team wins, the country wins; if the president signs, the whole country is bound. Jesus represents us in this active sense: his triumph over sin and death is our triumph.

elements.passageText:
18I consider that our present sufferings are not worth comparing with the glory that will be revealed in us. 19For the creation waits in eager expectation for the children of God to be revealed. 20For the creation was subjected to frustration, not by its own choice, but by the will of the one who subjected it, in hope 21that the creation itself will be liberated from its bondage to decay and brought into the freedom and glory of the children of God.

22We know that the whole creation has been groaning as in the pains of childbirth right up to the present time. 23Not only so, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for our adoption to sonship, the redemption of our bodies. 24For in this hope we were saved. But hope that is seen is no hope at all. Who hopes for what they already have? 25But if we hope for what we do not yet have, we wait for it patiently.

…

1Then I saw ‘a new heaven and a new earth,’ for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and there was no longer any sea. 2I saw the Holy City, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride beautifully dressed for her husband. 3And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying, ‘Look! God’s dwelling-place is now among the people, and he will dwell with them. They will be his people, and God himself will be with them and be their God. 4“He will wipe every tear from their eyes. There will be no more death” or mourning or crying or pain, for the old order of things has passed away.’

5He who was seated on the throne said, ‘I am making everything new!’ Then he said, ‘Write this down, for these words are trustworthy and true.’

elements.question: Romans 8 and Revelation 21 describe the same hope. What is creation doing now, and what will happen to it (Rom 8:19–22)? What do believers wait for (v23)? In Revelation 21, where does God make his home (v3), what is removed (v4), and what does he say he is doing with everything (v5)? Is the hope escape from the world, or its renewal?
elements.questionHint: Notice who is groaning, what they are waiting to be freed from and into, and where God ends up living.
elements.sampleAnswer: Creation groans like a woman in labour, waiting to be set free from decay into the freedom and glory of God’s children (Rom 8:19–22). Believers wait for the redemption of their bodies (v23). In Revelation God makes his home with people, wipes away every tear, and death, mourning, crying and pain are gone (Rev 21:3–4). He says he is making everything new (v5). The hope is renewal of creation, not escape from it.

elements.passageText: 13Brothers and sisters, we do not want you to be uninformed about those who sleep in death, so that you do not grieve like the rest of mankind, who have no hope. 14For we believe that Jesus died and rose again, and so we believe that God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep in him. 15According to the Lord’s word, we tell you that we who are still alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord, will certainly not precede those who have fallen asleep. 16For the Lord himself will come down from heaven, with a loud command, with the voice of the archangel and with the trumpet call of God, and the dead in Christ will rise first. 17After that, we who are still alive and are left will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air. And so we will be with the Lord for ever. 18Therefore encourage one another with these words.

elements.question: Paul does not tell the Thessalonians not to grieve. How does he say Christians grieve, and what is his reason (vv13–14)? What will happen, in order (vv15–17)?
elements.questionHint: Look at the contrast with the rest of mankind in verse 13.
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says they should not grieve like the rest of mankind, who have no hope (v13). The reason is that Jesus died and rose again, so God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep in him (v14). The Lord himself will come down from heaven, and the dead in Christ will rise first (v16). Then those who are still alive will be caught up with them, and so we will be with the Lord for ever (v17). Paul tells them to encourage one another with these words (v18).

elements.question: Which teaching of Jesus have I heard many times but not yet put into practice (Matt 7:24-27)?

Think of someone you are helping, and of 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18. Where in their life does it feel as if nothing can really be undone? Are they hoping for things to go back to how they were (resuscitation) or for something transformed (resurrection)?
In the light of Revelation 21:1–5, when we speak of heaven in our songs, sermons and funerals, do we speak of escape from creation, or of the resurrection of the body and a new creation?

elements.text:
Daniel doesn’t need to be told that the resurrection is true so much as shown what kind of truth it is. It isn’t a consolation prize set alongside real loss; it is God’s answer to real loss – not that death didn’t happen, but that death doesn’t have the last word. His grief is not a failure of faith: Christians grieve, but not without hope.

Look back at your answer about Daniel at the start. Has it changed? If you have time, you can read the accompanying book chapter to see how these passages fit together, and why the Resurrection is a good place to begin thinking about theology.

On Sunday mornings Naomi goes for a walk instead of going to church. She grew up in church but stopped attending in her second year at university. She now describes herself as ‘spiritual, not religious.’ She meditates, talks about ‘energy’ and ‘the universe,’ and finds church talk of sin and judgment cold by comparison. ‘At least when I sit outside and feel connected to everything,’ she says, ‘I feel that I’m part of something bigger than myself.’

Whether she realises it or not, Naomi has already made some important decisions about what creation is, and about how it relates to God – the subject of this chapter and the next. This chapter deals with the doctrine of creation ‘in general’ while the following chapter deals with the doctrine of the creation of humanity in particular. This chapter will first look at God’s act of creating, then at what this tells us about roles and responsibilities within creation, and then at the implications of creation for discipleship.

Naomi is a composite character, not a real individual.

elements.question: Naomi finds meaning in nature and feels ‘connected to everything.’ What is right about that, and what might be missing? Where do you see yourself, or people you know, in her story?
Before the next question, read the whole account of creation, aloud if you are in a group.
elements.answer:
1In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. 2Now the earth was formless and empty, darkness was over the surface of the deep, and the Spirit of God was hovering over the waters.

3And God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light. 4God saw that the light was good, and he separated the light from the darkness. 5God called the light ‘day’, and the darkness he called ‘night’. And there was evening, and there was morning – the first day.

6And God said, ‘Let there be a vault between the waters to separate water from water.’ 7So God made the vault and separated the water under the vault from the water above it. And it was so. 8God called the vault ‘sky’. And there was evening, and there was morning – the second day.

9And God said, ‘Let the water under the sky be gathered to one place, and let dry ground appear.’ And it was so. 10God called the dry ground ‘land’, and the gathered waters he called ‘seas’. And God saw that it was good.

11Then God said, ‘Let the land produce vegetation: seed-bearing plants and trees on the land that bear fruit with seed in it, according to their various kinds.’ And it was so. 12The land produced vegetation: plants bearing seed according to their kinds and trees bearing fruit with seed in it according to their kinds. And God saw that it was good. 13And there was evening, and there was morning – the third day.

14And God said, ‘Let there be lights in the vault of the sky to separate the day from the night, and let them serve as signs to mark sacred times, and days and years, 15and let them be lights in the vault of the sky to give light on the earth.’ And it was so. 16God made two great lights – the greater light to govern the day and the lesser light to govern the night. He also made the stars. 17God set them in the vault of the sky to give light on the earth, 18to govern the day and the night, and to separate light from darkness. And God saw that it was good. 19And there was evening, and there was morning – the fourth day.

20And God said, ‘Let the water teem with living creatures, and let birds fly above the earth across the vault of the sky.’ 21So God created the great creatures of the sea and every living thing with which the water teems and that moves about in it, according to their kinds, and every winged bird according to its kind. And God saw that it was good. 22God blessed them and said, ‘Be fruitful and increase in number and fill the water in the seas, and let the birds increase on the earth.’ 23And there was evening, and there was morning – the fifth day.

24And God said, ‘Let the land produce living creatures according to their kinds: the livestock, the creatures that move along the ground, and the wild animals, each according to its kind.’ And it was so. 25God made the wild animals according to their kinds, the livestock according to their kinds, and all the creatures that move along the ground according to their kinds. And God saw that it was good.

26Then God said, ‘Let us make mankind in our image, in our likeness, so that they may rule over the fish in the sea and the birds in the sky, over the livestock and all the wild animals, and over all the creatures that move along the ground.’

27So God created mankind in his own image,
in the image of God he created them;
male and female he created them.

28God blessed them and said to them, ‘Be fruitful and increase in number; fill the earth and subdue it. Rule over the fish in the sea and the birds in the sky and over every living creature that moves on the ground.’

29Then God said, ‘I give you every seed-bearing plant on the face of the whole earth and every tree that has fruit with seed in it. They will be yours for food. 30And to all the beasts of the earth and all the birds in the sky and all the creatures that move along the ground – everything that has the breath of life in it – I give every green plant for food.’ And it was so.

31God saw all that he had made, and it was very good. And there was evening, and there was morning – the sixth day.

2:1Thus the heavens and the earth were completed in all their vast array.

2By the seventh day God had finished the work he had been doing; so on the seventh day he rested from all his work. 3Then God blessed the seventh day and made it holy, because on it he rested from all the work of creating that he had done.

elements.text: As you read, notice who acts, how God creates, what he calls ‘good’, and what is missing from the account. Many ancient stories of origins involve battles between gods; look for any sign of a rival here.

elements.question: What stands out to you in Genesis 1? What does it tell us about God, and about the world he made?

elements.passageText:
1In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. 2Now the earth was formless and empty, darkness was over the surface of the deep, and the Spirit of God was hovering over the waters.

3And God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light. 4God saw that the light was good, and he separated the light from the darkness. 5God called the light ‘day’, and the darkness he called ‘night’. And there was evening, and there was morning – the first day.

elements.question: How does God bring light into being (v3), and what does that suggest about his power? What do you notice about the Spirit’s role in verse 2?
elements.questionHint: Look at what God does before light appears, and at what he does not use.
elements.sampleAnswer: God speaks, and light comes into being (v3): his word alone is enough. Nothing in the passage shows him struggling against a rival or needing a tool, which shows how great his power is. In verse 2 the Spirit of God is already there, hovering over the waters before the light appears. So creation is God’s work, with his Spirit present from the beginning.

elements.passageText:
6By the word of the [[sc:Lord]] the heavens were made,
their starry host by the breath of his mouth.
7He gathers the waters of the sea into jars;
he puts the deep into storehouses.
8Let all the earth fear the [[sc:Lord]];
let all the people of the world revere him.
9For he spoke, and it came to be;
he commanded, and it stood firm.

elements.question: How does Psalm 33:6–9 describe creation, and how does it connect to Genesis 1:3? What response does the psalm call for (v8)?
elements.questionHint: Notice the verbs: he spoke, he commanded.
elements.sampleAnswer: The psalm says the heavens were made by the word of the Lord, and their starry host by the breath of his mouth (v6). This echoes Genesis 1:3, where God speaks and things come to be: he spoke, and it came to be (v9). He also gathers the waters of the sea and puts the deep into storehouses (v7), so even the sea is under his control. The right response is that all the earth should fear the Lord and all the people of the world should revere him (v8).

elements.passageText:
1In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. 2He was with God in the beginning. 3Through him all things were made; without him nothing was made that has been made.

…

6yet for us there is but one God, the Father, from whom all things came and for whom we live; and there is but one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came and through whom we live.

…

15The Son is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn over all creation. 16For in him all things were created: things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or powers or rulers or authorities; all things have been created through him and for him. 17He is before all things, and in him all things hold together.

elements.question: What does each passage say about the Son’s part in creation, and how does it relate him to the Father? Looking back at Genesis 1:2, where would you look for the Spirit?
elements.questionHint: Look for the little words through, for and in.
elements.sampleAnswer: John says the Word was with God and was God, and that all things were made through him (John 1:1–3). Paul says there is one God, the Father, from whom all things came, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came (1 Cor 8:6). In Colossians the Son is the image of the invisible God, all things were created through him and for him, and in him all things hold together (Col 1:15–17). The Spirit appears in Genesis 1:2, hovering over the waters, so creation is the work of Father, Son and Spirit together.

elements.passageText:
31God saw all that he had made, and it was very good. And there was evening, and there was morning – the sixth day.

2:1Thus the heavens and the earth were completed in all their vast array.

2By the seventh day God had finished the work he had been doing; so on the seventh day he rested from all his work. 3Then God blessed the seventh day and made it holy, because on it he rested from all the work of creating that he had done.

elements.question: Look back over Genesis 1. How often does God call his work ‘good’, and what changes in verse 31? What does the rest on the seventh day (2:1–3) tell us about God’s relationship to what he has made?
elements.questionHint: Count the ‘good’s, then compare the last verdict.
elements.sampleAnswer: God calls his work good six times, in verses 4, 10, 12, 18, 21 and 25, and in verse 31 he calls all that he had made very good. So the physical world is good, and is not a mistake or a trap. In 2:1–3 the work is completed, and God rests on the seventh day, blesses it and makes it holy. Creation is finished and ordered, and God is at rest in what he has made.

elements.question: Have you ever heard that spiritual things are better than physical ones, and that the body or the material world is somehow lower, or even evil? Look back at Genesis 1 before you answer, then tap ‘Find out’.
elements.answer: Gnosticism was an early Christian heresy that saw physical existence as evil. It taught that a lesser, evil god (the ‘demiurge’) made the material world, and that salvation meant escaping it through secret ‘knowledge’. Genesis says the opposite: the one true God made everything and calls it good, even very good. The Bible does not treat the physical world as a trap to escape, and the Son took a body.

elements.passageText:
24‘The God who made the world and everything in it is the Lord of heaven and earth and does not live in temples built by human hands. 25And he is not served by human hands, as if he needed anything. Rather, he himself gives everyone life and breath and everything else. 26From one man he made all the nations, that they should inhabit the whole earth; and he marked out their appointed times in history and the boundaries of their lands. 27God did this so that they would seek him and perhaps reach out for him and find him, though he is not far from any one of us. 28“For in him we live and move and have our being.” As some of your own poets have said, “We are his offspring.”

…

3The Son is the radiance of God’s glory and the exact representation of his being, sustaining all things by his powerful word. After he had provided purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty in heaven.

…

10He also says,

‘In the beginning, Lord, you laid the foundations of the earth,
and the heavens are the work of your hands.

elements.question: What does God give to everyone, and what does he not need (Acts 17:24–25)? What does it mean that ‘in him we live and move and have our being’ (v28)? What do Hebrews 1:3 and 1:10 say the Son has done and is doing? (Hebrews 1:10 is addressed to the Son.)
elements.questionHint: Look at the direction of the giving: who gives, and who receives?
elements.sampleAnswer: God gives everyone life and breath and everything else, and he needs nothing from us, because he is not served by human hands as if he needed anything (Acts 17:25). To say that in him we live and move and have our being is to say that we depend on him at every moment, not only at the beginning. Hebrews says the Son laid the foundations of the earth (1:10) and is now sustaining all things by his powerful word (1:3). Creation is not a one-off event: everything continues to depend on him.

elements.passageText:
1The heavens declare the glory of God;
the skies proclaim the work of his hands.
2Day after day they pour forth speech;
night after night they reveal knowledge.
3They have no speech, they use no words;
no sound is heard from them.
4Yet their voice goes out into all the earth,
their words to the ends of the world.
In the heavens God has pitched a tent for the sun.
5It is like a bridegroom coming out of his chamber,
like a champion rejoicing to run his course.
6It rises at one end of the heavens
and makes its circuit to the other;
nothing is deprived of its warmth.

…

11‘You are worthy, our Lord and God,
to receive glory and honour and power,
for you created all things,
and by your will they were created
and have their being.’

elements.question: What are the heavens doing (Ps 19:1–4), and why, according to Revelation 4:11, were all things created? What does that suggest creation is for?
elements.questionHint: Notice who the heavens are talking about, and who is worthy to receive in Revelation 4:11.
elements.sampleAnswer: The heavens declare the glory of God and proclaim the work of his hands (Ps 19:1). Day after day and night after night they pour forth speech and reveal knowledge, though they use no words (vv2–3), and their voice goes out into all the earth (v4). In Revelation 4:11 God is worthy to receive glory, honour and power, because he created all things and by his will they were created and have their being. So creation exists for God’s glory: it points to him, and he deserves the praise.

elements.question: Whose earth is it (Ps 24:1–2)? What place does Psalm 8 give to human beings (vv3–8), and what does the psalm assume about who is really in charge (v9)? What would that mean for how we treat what we think we own?
elements.questionHint: Look at whose earth it is, then at what human beings are given in Psalm 8.
elements.sampleAnswer: The earth belongs to the Lord, and so does everything in it, because he founded it on the seas (Ps 24:1–2). Psalm 8 says human beings are made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honour, and made rulers over the works of God’s hands (vv5–6). But the psalm ends by praising the Lord whose name is majestic in all the earth (v9), so human beings rule under him. We are stewards, not owners: responsible for what we have been given, and accountable to the one it belongs to.

elements.question: Thinking of Psalm 24:1–2 and Psalm 8: do I treat my body, my work or my possessions as something to escape, to worship, or to own, rather than to steward? Which is my greatest temptation?

Think of someone you are helping, and of Acts 17:24–28 and Hebrews 1:3. Do they attribute too much meaning to nature (worship), or too little (dismissal)? Where might they be acting as an owner rather than as a steward?
Think of our church, and of Psalm 19:1–6 and Revelation 4:11. Do our prayers and songs thank God for creation (food, rain, bodies, seasons) as well as for salvation?

elements.text:
Naomi is half right. Genesis agrees that the world is full of meaning and worthy of wonder – but as a gift, not as God himself. If everything is simply ‘the universe’, there is no one left to thank. The God of Genesis keeps the difference between Creator and creation, and in keeping it makes room for a real relationship. Her sense of belonging to something bigger than herself can become a pointer to the Creator she was made to know (Rom 1:20).

Look back at your answer about Naomi at the start. Has it changed? If you have time, you can read the accompanying book chapter to see how these passages fit together, and what follows for worship, stewardship and the way we think about evil.

opening.body:
*Wake up, sleeper, rise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.* (Ephesians 5:14)

Daniel’s wife died eight months ago after a short illness.[[fn:1]] He still comes to church every week, sits in the same place, and sings the songs – but something in him has gone quiet. ‘I believe in the resurrection,’ he tells his pastor. ‘I just don’t feel that it changes anything. She’s still gone. The house is still empty. I can’t see how any of that is going to be undone.’

Whether he realises it or not, Daniel is facing a question of theology: how what he believes connects with how he lives and grieves – the subject of this chapter.

awakeningToTheology.body:
> Remember, therefore, what you have received and heard; hold it fast, and repent.\
> But if you do not wake up, I will come like a thief,\
> and you will not know at what time I will come to you. (Rev 3:3)

Everybody is some sort of theologian. The issue is not *whether* we have a theology. No matter who we are – Christian, atheist, Muslim, Buddhist, or agnostic – we all have a theology, even before we awake to the fact. We all have some sort of idea of how we would answer the big questions of life: Is there a God? What is God like? How do we know what is right and wrong? What does it mean to be a human being? What happens to a person at death? Everyone has an answer to those questions (even if the answer is ‘I don’t know’ or ‘Nothing is there’). So the issue is not *whether* we have a theology, but rather whether we *reflect* on the theology we already have. Do we develop a reflective theology, or do we stick with an unreflective theology?

That is why I am using the metaphor of ‘waking.’ When you awaken to the tasks of a new day, the day does not spring into being when you wake. The day is already in process, and you are already part of it, even in your sleep. Your awakening allows you to join in with the day, consciously and reflectively. It is similar with theology. Your theology is already in process, and you are already thinking theologically, long before you reflect on what you are doing. In choosing to study theology, you are not *starting* the process of becoming a theologian. You already *are* a theologian, by existing as a creature in God’s image, in his world. Instead, in choosing to study theology, you are *awakening* to the fact that you already are a theologian – perhaps awakening to this for the very first time, or perhaps awakening more fully to something you have begun to grasp previously.

The Christian life is theological through and through. Whenever you ask, or answer, ‘Who is God?’, ‘What does it mean to have faith?’ or ‘What is sin?’, you are doing theology.

When you seek to know God better, you are doing theology. When you try to please him, you are putting theology into practice. All of us are theologians; the only question is whether we are ‘good’ or ‘bad’ theologians – do we seek to know God well, or badly? Are we reflective or unreflective theologians; are we growing or stagnant theologians? If we take God seriously, then we will want to be reflective about our theology, and growing in our theology – we will want to be doing our theology *well*.

definingTheology.body: ‘Theology’ and ‘doctrine’ are often used interchangeably, and in this book I treat them as synonyms unless a distinction matters. Strictly, though, they differ. Doctrine (from the Latin *doctrina*, ‘teaching’) is the attempt to clarify and pass on the core teachings of the Christian faith. Theology (from the Greek *theos*, ‘God’, and *logos*, ‘word’ or ‘study’) is the study of God. More formally, it is the systematic study of Christian teaching, which seeks a clear understanding of reality, expressed in terms that our own world, cultures and lives can grasp, and with its relevance to them made clear.[[fn:2]] So, loosely, the two words can be used interchangeably; more precisely, Christian theology is the systematic study of Christian doctrine.

howTheologyConnects.body:
Theology connects. Theological ideas don’t just lie around haphazardly, like a heap of random bricks on the ground. But the connections are complex. Developing Christian theology is less like building a wall, as in Figure 1.1 (where each row of bricks builds sequentially on the row below it), and more like constructing a spider’s web, as in Figure 1.2 (where every part is connected to every part).

*(Figures 1.1 and 1.2 are in the Figures at the end of this chapter.)*

The metaphor (or conceptual model) we use for understanding how theology connects makes a difference to how we see theological errors. If you knock one brick out of a wall, the rest of the wall may be essentially unaffected – perhaps it will be a little weaker where the hole is, but the overall shape of the wall is unchanged. But if you snap one strand of a spider’s web, it distorts the whole web – if you snap a major strand, the whole web is distorted massively, or maybe even destroyed; if you snap a minor strand, the whole web is still distorted, but perhaps more subtly.

The interconnections between topics in theology will not be quite so regular as the spider’s web in Figure 1.2 suggests. Figure 1.4 gives an example of how these connections might look if presented in the form of a mind map.

This interconnected, web-like nature is hard to convey in a book, because books are naturally meant to be read in a linear order. You start at chapter 1, then move on to chapter 2, and so on. Reading a book is more like following the bricks in a wall – that is just how books work. So the chapters in this book will follow a logical order (partly shaped around the biblical storyline from Creation to Fall to Salvation to New Creation). However, I am not assuming that we are building a wall from scratch. I assume that my readers are already familiar with the basic contours of Christian theology, so that reading this book is actually more like another journey round the spider’s web. Because of this, I will, from time to time, point out the connections between one part of theology and another.

theologyAndDiscipleship.body:
Scripture never separates the truth we believe from the life we live. Jesus says that the truth will set us free (John 8:32), and prays that his disciples will be sanctified by it (John 17:17). Whoever ‘lives by the truth comes into the light’ (John 3:21), and as we speak ‘the truth in love’ we grow to maturity in Christ (Eph 4:15). Paul describes his own calling as furthering ‘the faith of God’s elect and their knowledge of the truth that leads to godliness’ (Titus 1:1). That is the point of knowing the truth: it is meant to lead to godliness. Knowledge of the truth that does not lead to godliness is foolishness. Jesus puts it this way:

> ‘Therefore everyone who hears these words of mine and puts them into practice is like a wise man who built his house on the rock. The rain came down, the streams rose, and the winds blew and beat against that house; yet it did not fall, because it had its foundation on the rock. But everyone who hears these words of mine and does not put them into practice is like a foolish man who built his house on sand. The rain came down, the streams rose, and the winds blew and beat against that house, and it fell with a great crash.’ (Matt 7:24-27)

The parable distinguishes wise people from foolish people. But the difference is not exposure to the truth – in the parable *both* the wise man *and* the foolish man represent people who ‘hear these words’ of Jesus. The difference is not the hearing, but *what you do with* the hearing. To study theology, without your life being changed, is to be like the foolish man building his house on the sand. That’s not a good place to be. God’s truth is meant to lead us to godliness. Doctrine is meant for discipleship.[[fn:3]] In Titus 2 Paul takes us to the heart of theology, ‘the grace of God’ that has appeared (Titus 2:11), and what he says of that grace applies to theology as a whole:

> It teaches us to say ‘No’ to ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright and godly lives in this present age, while we wait for the blessed hope – the appearing of the glory of our great God and Saviour, Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us to redeem us from all wickedness and to purify for himself a people that are his very own, eager to do what is good. (Titus 2:12-14)

*Lord, make me to know you aright, that I may love, serve, enjoy and possess you more and more.\
And since in the life below I cannot fully attain this blessedness,\
let it at least grow in me day by day, until it all be fulfilled in the life to come. Amen.*\
(Adapted from Anselm of Canterbury, *Proslogion* 26)[[fn:4]]

extrasExegesisToEthics.body:
There can be value in having different perspectives on how progressive revelation unfolds. From the perspective of exegesis and biblical theology it can be useful to think of Scripture as drama, where you move from one Act to the next – and so you generally leave one to enter the next – the exception being the New Testament era, which is then described as an ‘overlap of the ages.’[[fn:5]]

From the perspective of ethics, however, it can be helpful to think more in terms of layers – when you are standing on one layer, you are also at the same time standing on all the other layers that came before. (Imagine standing on a rug: you are being held up by the rug, *and* being held up by the concrete under the rug, *and* being held up by the ground under the concrete.) From this perspective, as New Testament believers we are in the new age, and at the same time we are still in the old creation – and so our experience reflects both realities at once.

(Thanks to Tim Adeney for this clarification.)

whereToStart.body: If we thought theology was like a brick wall – with one row as a foundation, and the next row on top of it and so on – then it might be very important to know where to start. We might need to decide which topics go on the bottom row, and which topics come next and so on. But if theology is more like a web, or an interconnected network, then it does not matter quite so much where we start.[[fn:6]] We will need to cover every topic eventually, and preferably we will cover them several times. What is more important is that we keep developing the network of interconnections – we need to keep considering how each part of theology relates to every other part, and we need to think about which parts are most closely connected, and thus which parts are most interdependent on each other. For example, the way we understand the person of Christ will affect the way we understand the work of Christ, and vice versa. Similarly, the way we understand the incarnation will influence the way we understand the Trinity and vice versa.

whyResurrection.body:
The Resurrection of Jesus Christ might seem a strange place to start: it comes in the middle of the story, not at the beginning. But it takes us to the centre of God’s purposes, and the New Testament itself starts here.[[fn:7]]

When the apostles first preached the gospel, the Resurrection stood at its centre (Acts 2:24, 32; 17:31). When Paul sums up what he passed on ‘as of first importance,’ it is that Christ died for our sins, was buried, and ‘was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures’ (1 Cor 15:3-4). And he makes everything hang on it: ‘if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile; you are still in your sins’ (1 Cor 15:17). Peter, too, opens his first letter with the living hope that the Resurrection gives (1 Pet 1:3).

Starting with the Resurrection is not an attempt to isolate the Resurrection from other key moments in salvation history. In fact, the Resurrection makes a good starting point precisely because it is so fundamentally connected with so much of the rest of theology. Consider the following seven-point summary of the Bible’s message:

- God created the world, and originally the world was entirely and beautifully good.

- Humanity sinned, rebelling against God, and bringing death, suffering, and brokenness into the world.

- God entered our experience, becoming a human being, incarnated in the person of his Son, Jesus.

- Jesus became our representative: he died for the sins of the world, bearing the punishment for all our wrong-doing, in our place.

- God raised Jesus from the dead, physically and definitively, so that death is defeated; he currently reigns with God.

- Jesus will come again to right all wrongs, and to usher in a new heaven and a new earth.

- God’s redeemed people will reign with him forever in a new universe where everything is finally made right.

All of those points need each other in order to make complete sense. And the Resurrection only makes sense when understood in the light of all the others: The Resurrection is the affirmation of the goodness of God’s original creation, even in the light of human sin. It is only possible because of the incarnation, and because of Jesus standing as our atoning representative. The Resurrection declares that Jesus’ atoning work on the cross is complete. At the cross God pronounced his ‘No’ to sinful life in the flesh, and that ‘No’ was the condition of his ‘Yes’ to redeemed life in the Spirit, which he declared in raising Jesus from the dead.[[fn:8]] But this life in the Spirit is a spiritual physicality – Jesus’ Resurrection is the firstfruits of a whole New Creation, where everything will be renewed, perfected and made right. Paul’s ‘spiritual body’ (1 Cor 15:44) is a body transformed by the Spirit, not an immaterial one. His Resurrection gives us a glimpse of what the whole New Creation will be like – it is a foretaste of it. Jesus himself will return as Judge to usher in this new heaven and new earth, and all God’s people will be resurrected, just as he has been, and will reign with him forever in this new world where everything is finally made right.

The Resurrection of Christ inverts an inversion.[[fn:9]] Sin and death turned God’s good world upside down; the Resurrection turns it the right way up again. It takes a situation that is very wrong and puts it right – yet not as a simple reset, back to square one, but by transforming it into something better than it was before. Daniel’s empty house is exactly the kind of wrong that seems beyond undoing. And yet the Resurrection gives hope that one day it will be undone.

In the Resurrection, God reverses Adam’s choice of sin and death and reaffirms God’s initial gift to Adam of goodness and life: ‘For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive’ (1 Cor 15:22). But this reaffirmation is not just a repeat of that original affirmation in Genesis 1. The Resurrection of Christ goes beyond that original gift of life, and transforms it. Paul points to this truth when he argues that the ‘last Adam’ (Jesus) is parallel to, but greater than the first Adam: ‘“The first man Adam became a living being”; the last Adam, a life-giving spirit’ (1 Cor 15:45).

The Resurrection also reaffirms God’s initial work as Creator. Without Jesus’ Resurrection, we could have had some grounds for wondering whether God’s initial good creation was irreparably ruined. The first big-scale response to sin in Genesis is the story of the Flood – which is almost like an Uncreation Event: the separations of Genesis 1 are undone, and the world returns to its initial ‘watery deep’ state (Gen 1:2, NET). This seems to be the equivalent of a hard reboot – and yet even this drastic event does not deal with sin: afterwards, ‘every inclination of the human heart is evil from childhood’ (Gen 8:21). The question naturally arises: If even the Flood is not big enough to deal with sin, then can *anything* reverse the damage that was done at the Fall? Is creation a lost cause? ‘If the creature consistently acted to uncreate itself, and with itself to uncreate the rest of creation, did this not mean that God’s handiwork was flawed beyond hope of repair? It might have been possible before Christ rose from the dead to answer in good faith, Yes.’[[fn:10]]

extrasSolidPhysicalHope.header: Extras: Our hope is solid and physical
extrasSolidPhysicalHope.body:
Without the Resurrection, then, perhaps the ‘best’ salvation we could have hoped for would have been some sort of redemption *from* creation, rather than the redemption *of* creation.[[fn:11]] This is sometimes called a ‘gnostic’ hope – a hope to escape from the physical creation into some sort of ‘spiritual-only’ afterlife. (I will return to ‘gnosticism’ briefly in Chapter 2.)

Christians, too, can slip into a ‘gnostic’ hope instead of a fully Christian one. In the West you see this in cartoons of ‘heaven’ as fluffy white clouds, with people floating around in white robes, holding harps. In Africa the same hope can take another form. Traditional belief holds that ‘at death, one moves into the presence of the ancestors,’ and the dead are spoken of as ‘the living dead.’[[fn:12]] We need to make sure that the hope held out at Christian funerals is more than just rest, or just joining those who have gone before. Both pictures have given up on the goodness of creation: they look for life after death, but not for the resurrection of the body. The Resurrection tells us that human sin will not be allowed to uncreate what God has created. His New Creation will triumph.

extrasRepresentation.body:
In the Resurrection, just as in the atonement, Jesus is our representative. He stands in our place.

We use the word ‘representation’ in at least two different ways, so it is good to be clear about exactly what we mean. Representation can be symbolic (only), and representation can also be active.

A football team can be represented by its logo (or its team colours); a country can be represented by its flag. This is symbolic representation: the flag (or logo/colours) don’t have to do anything – they just symbolise what they represent.

Active representation is different. When a country’s football team goes to the World Cup, those 11 players represent all the citizens of that country. The 11 players act on behalf of the country: if the players win, the country wins. When a country’s president goes to the UN, the president represents all the citizens of that country. If the president signs a treaty, the whole country is bound by it.

The Resurrection is not merely symbolic representation – it is much more active than that. Jesus’ fate is our fate. His triumph over sin and death is our triumph over sin and death. His restoration is our restoration. His Resurrection guarantees our resurrection to come.

summary.body:
1. Everyone already has a theology. The question is whether we reflect on it and grow in it – whether we are good theologians or bad ones.

2. ‘Doctrine’ and ‘theology’ can be used interchangeably. More precisely, theology is the systematic study of Christian doctrine, made clear and relevant to our world.

3. Theology connects. It is less like a brick wall, built row by row, and more like a spider’s web, where a broken strand distorts the whole.

4. Exegesis, biblical theology, systematic theology and ethics form a flow, and we may need to go round it more than once.

5. Knowing the truth is meant to lead to godliness (Titus 1:1). Doctrine is for discipleship: to hear Jesus’ words without putting them into practice is to build on sand (Matt 7:24-27).

6. Because theology is a web, it matters less where we start. This book starts with the Resurrection. There God reverses Adam’s choice of sin and death and reaffirms his creation, and the new life goes beyond the first gift of life.

7. Our hope is the redemption of creation, not redemption from it. In his resurrection, as in his death, Jesus is our active representative: his victory over sin and death is ours.

toolsMyself.header: Tools for Making Disciples: For myself
toolsMyself.body:
The doctrine of the Resurrection is meant to shape how we live, not only what we believe, and these prompts take it in three directions: towards myself, towards someone I am helping, and towards our church.

- Which of my beliefs about God, death or right and wrong have I held for years without ever stopping to examine them?

- Is my faith more like a wall or a web? If one belief were shaken, what else would I feel was at risk?

- Which teaching of Jesus have I heard many times but not yet put into practice (Matt 7:24-27)?

- Do I hope for the redemption of creation, or for an escape from it? What difference does Jesus’ bodily resurrection make to how I think about my body, my work and my death?

toolsSomeoneElse.header: Tools for Making Disciples: For someone I am helping
toolsSomeoneElse.body:
Begin by listening to the person’s story and reasons: these prompts are for opening a conversation, not for diagnosing someone from a distance, and they help to locate where Resurrection hope has, or has not yet, reached a particular situation.

- Where in this person’s life does it feel as if nothing can really be undone?

- Are they hoping for mere resuscitation (things going back to how they were), or for resurrection (things transformed into something greater)?

- What would change if they trusted that, because Jesus has been raised, God’s ‘no’ to death and decay is final and certain – even while grief remains?

- Is their theology currently a wall (one crack and it all comes down) or a web (still connected, even under strain)?

toolsChurch.header: Tools for Making Disciples: For our church
toolsChurch.body:
- When we speak of heaven in our songs, sermons and funerals, do we speak of escape from creation, or of the resurrection of the body and a new creation?

- How do we stay with the bereaved after the funeral is over, when the visits stop but the grief does not?

- Do we make room for honest questions and help people think them through, or do we treat questions as a lack of faith?

- How do we judge whether our teaching is working: by how much people know, or by whether what they know is leading to godliness (Titus 1:1)?

danielRevisited.body:
When Daniel says that he believes in the resurrection but does not feel that it changes anything, it is tempting to move straight to reassurance – ‘she’s in a better place,’ ‘you’ll see her again.’ These may be true things, but said too quickly they can sound like a request for Daniel to feel better, rather than help for him to grieve.

Daniel does not need to be told that the resurrection is true so much as shown what kind of truth it is. The Resurrection of Jesus is not a consolation prize set alongside real loss. It is God’s answer to real loss: not that death did not happen, but that death does not have the last word (1 Cor 15:54-57). Because Christ was raised bodily, the hope held out to Daniel is not a vague survival but the resurrection of the body – the undoing of the very thing he says cannot be undone.

Daniel’s grief is not a failure of faith. Christians grieve, but not ‘like the rest of mankind, who have no hope’ (1 Thess 4:13). His pastor’s task is to grieve with him, and to keep that hope in view until Daniel can hold it again for himself.

questionsForReflection.body:
1. What would you say to Daniel – and what would you avoid saying?

2. Should every Christian study theology? Why, or why not?

3. How much theology is ‘enough’ for you to know?

4. The chapter compares theology to a brick wall and to a spider’s web. Which picture better describes how you currently think about theology – and what would change if you adopted the other?

5. Why does this book start with the Resurrection rather than, say, the doctrine of God? What does that choice teach about how to do theology?

6. Titus 1:1 links knowledge of the truth with godliness. Where in your own life has your knowledge of God not yet shaped your godliness – and why?

technicalTerms.body:
Doctrine: the core teachings of the Christian faith, clarified and passed on (from Latin *doctrina*, teaching).

Theology: the systematic study of Christian teaching, aiming at a clear understanding of reality that is comprehensible, and relevant, within our contemporary world (from Greek *theos*, God, and *logos*, word or study).

Systematic theology: theology that gathers what the whole Bible teaches on a subject and relates it to the rest of Christian belief.

Representation: either symbolic (a flag represents a country) or active (a team represents a country by acting on its behalf). Jesus is our active representative in his death and Resurrection.

Gnostic hope: a hope of redemption from creation, rather than the redemption of creation. The term is borrowed from O’Donovan; it names a kind of hope, not the whole of ancient Gnosticism.

A full, readable evangelical systematic theology. Chapters 1-4 ask what theology is, whether it is possible, how it is done, and how it is contextualised. For students, pastors, and serious lay readers.

A systematic theology written for African contexts, setting biblical teaching beside traditional African worldviews. Chapter 10, ‘Death, Judgement and Eternity,’ covers death, burial and the afterlife, and the resurrection of the dead; chapter 7 discusses reverence for ancestors. For students and pastors.

**McGrath, Alister E. *Christian Theology: An Introduction*.** 6th ed. Chichester: Wiley Blackwell, 2017.\
