opening.body:
*You alone are the [[sc:Lord]]. You made the heavens, even the highest heavens, and all their starry host,\
the earth and all that is on it, the seas and all that is in them.\
You give life to everything, and the multitudes of heaven worship you.*

Nehemiah 9:6

*An error concerning the Creation ends as false thinking about God*.

(Thomas Aquinas)[[fn:1]]

On Sunday mornings Naomi goes for a walk instead of going to church. She grew up in church but stopped attending in her second year at university.[[fn:2]] She now describes herself as ‘spiritual, not religious.’ She meditates, talks about ‘energy’ and ‘the universe,’ and finds church talk of sin and judgment cold by comparison. ‘At least when I sit outside and feel connected to everything,’ she says, ‘I feel that I’m part of something bigger than myself.’

Whether she realises it or not, Naomi has already made some important decisions about what creation is, and about how it relates to God – the subject of this chapter and the next. This chapter deals with the doctrine of creation ‘in general’ while the following chapter deals with the doctrine of the creation of *humanity* in particular. This chapter will first look at God’s *act* of creating, then at what this tells us about roles and responsibilities within creation, and then at the implications of creation for discipleship.

extrasOtherOriginStoriesViolence.body:
There are many alternative origin stories, both ancient and modern. Many of them share something missing from Genesis 1: conflict and (often gory) violence.[[fn:3]] Such accounts thus see a dualism between good and evil, or else an indifference between them, as basic to reality.

In Genesis, however, God is supreme, so there is no rival for him to be in conflict with. The cosmos is created through peaceful speech not the carnage of war. So when we seek peace we are not chasing a pipe-dream; we are calling our world back to its origins, however obscured they may currently be.

(A later volume will explore the profound implications of having a Trinitarian God as Creator.)

theActOfCreating.body: This section considers how God creates: from *nothing* to something; from nothing to something *good*; and from nothing to something well-*ordered*.

fromNothingToSomething.body:
‘In the beginning, God.’ Scripture teaches that God alone is eternal. For the rest of creation, there was a time[[fn:4]] when it did not exist. Everything else has a start, but God does not. The technical term for this is to say that God created *ex nihilo*, which means ‘out of nothing.’[[fn:5]] This rules out two false understandings:

1. **Dualism**. Some pagan religions believed in ‘dualism’ – i.e. that Good and Evil were equal and opposite. A Christianised (and syncretistic) version of this would be to believe that God expresses the eternal and omnipresent principle of Good, and that Satan expresses the eternal and omnipresent principle of Evil.[[fn:6]] The Bible is completely different from these pagan myths. God alone is Creator; there is no dualism of any sort. God did not have to overcome any hostile force in order to create. Before God created, there wasn’t anything else other than God. There wasn’t even ‘God plus nothing’ (as if ‘nothing’ was a sort of ‘pseudo-something’). There was just God.

2. **Emanation**. The world is not an ‘emanation’ from God – as if God made the world out of himself (rather than out of nothing), as if it was somehow an extension of his being. The world is ‘other’ than God. God is immanent, but remains transcendent.

This original act of divine creation, in Genesis 1:1, is unique, and uniquely expresses God’s sovereignty and power. (Sometimes this ‘creation *ex nihilo*’ is referred to as ‘primary creation.’)[[fn:7]] God, of course, continues to create throughout the rest of Genesis 1, but in the rest of the chapter he is shaping the universe that he has already called into being out of nothingness. (This ‘shaping-creation’ is sometimes referred to as ‘secondary creation.’)

#### God’s power

extrasDeismPantheism.body:
**Deism** (from the Latin deus meaning ‘god’) is the belief that God created the world, but has now withdrawn from it. He cannot (or does not) engage with his creation. Deism stresses transcendence and denies immanence.

**Pantheism** (from the Greek πᾶν or pan, meaning ‘all’ and θεός or theos, meaning ‘god’) is the belief that God is everything and everything is God: God *is* the universe and the universe *is* God (or, at least, the universe is an emanation of God). A pantheistic God is not personal. Pantheism stresses immanence and denies transcendence.

**Panentheism** (from the Greek πᾶν or pan meaning ‘all,’ ἐν or en meaning ‘in,’ and θεός or theos meaning ‘god’ – so altogether meaning ‘all-in-God’) is a close relative of pantheism. It is the belief that the world exists within God, but that God is ‘bigger’ than the world. Forms of it differ on how far the world is itself divine.

fromNothingToSomethingContinued.body:
God created the whole universe out of nothing, and called it into existence. This gives us a glimpse of his power. Four other truths help unpack this power:

- **God is not dependent**. He existed before creation, and without it. He doesn’t depend on it, it depends on him.

- **God is not local**. He created absolutely everything there is. Every galaxy, every planet, every country, every region. He is God over everything, and everyone.

- **God is transcendent**. Transcendence refers to God being above and beyond the universe. God is wholly other to creation, wholly distinct from it, not simply some aspect of it. God’s radical, divine holiness is one way the Bible speaks of his transcendence.

- **God is immanent**. Immanence refers to God being and acting within the universe. He is in communion with the world that he has created. God continuously sustains the world. He is active within it, and it is entirely dependent on his presence: ‘In him we live and move and have our being’ (Acts 17:28).

#### The power of his Word

In particular, the act of creation shows us the power of God’s word: ‘And God said … and it was so.’ Seven times in Genesis 1, God speaks and things come to be, just the way he said for them to be. For us creatures, if we want something to happen then speaking is generally not enough; we have to physically *do* something. Not so with God: ‘By the word of the [[sc:Lord]] the heavens were made, their starry host by the breath of his mouth. … For he spoke, and it came to be; he commanded, and it stood firm’ (Ps 33:6, 9). Even the ongoing existence of the universe depends on the divine word: the Son sustains all things by his powerful word (Heb 1:3).

#### The role of the Son and the Spirit

The act of creation is a Trinitarian act. Certainly God the Father is the God of creation: ‘there is but one God, the Father, from whom all things came and for whom we live’ (1 Cor 8:6a). The Son is also intimately involved in creation: ‘there is but one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came and through whom we live’ (1 Cor 8:6b). He is the Word who speaks creation into existence (cf. John 1:1-3), and he is the one through whom and for whom everything is created (Col 1:15-17) – the Son is also the God of creation. The Spirit too is intimately involved in creation – he is the Spirit who hovers over the newly formed creation from the beginning, superintending it (cf. Gen 1:2; Job 26:13, 33:4; Ps 104:30; Isa 40:12-13) – the Spirit is also the God of creation.

fromNothingToSomethingGood.body: Unlike gnosticism and paganism, the Bible teaches us that the physical world of matter is not evil. God repeatedly affirms it as ‘good’ – even as ‘very good.’

extrasGnosticismTheDemiurge.body:
**Gnosticism** (from the Greek γνωστικός or gnōstikós, meaning ‘having knowledge’) was an early Christian heresy. It emphasised personal spiritual knowledge (‘gnosis’) instead of apostolic teachings, and church authority. It viewed physical existence as evil. Salvation was thought to involve direct ‘knowledge’ of God through mystical ‘insight.’ Instead of focusing on sin and repentance, Gnosticism spoke of illusion and enlightenment. Gnostics believed in a supreme, hidden God who was responsible for spirituality and goodness, and a lesser, evil god who was responsible for creating the physical universe.

**Demiurge** (from the Greek δημιουργός or dēmiourgós, meaning ‘artisan’ or ‘craftsman’) was a term originally used in Greek Platonic philosophy as roughly equivalent in meaning to creator. The Gnostics, however, adopted the term and used it to refer to their idea of a lesser, evil god who they thought had created the physical universe.

fromNothingToSomethingGoodContinued.body:
However, it is worth noticing that ‘good’ is not the same as ‘perfect.’ This is not to disparage the original creation – after all, in God’s own estimate it is *very* good! But it is to take account of three important biblical truths. First of all, ‘good’ (and ‘very good’) is the Bible’s own language for describing the creation; ‘perfect’ is not.[[fn:8]] Second, the Fall could happen. It is easier to talk about a ‘very good’ world going wrong, than to talk about a ‘perfect’ world going wrong. (‘If it was perfect, why did it go wrong in the first place??’) Third, the New Creation will be even better than the original (not least because no ‘Second Fall’ will be possible). So the original creation was very good, and the New Creation will be even better.[[fn:9]] If we were going to use the language of ‘perfect’ in regard to creation, we would be better to save it for speaking of the New Creation.[[fn:10]]

#### God’s love and generosity

God chose to create the universe out of love. Creation is an act of self-giving by God. He did not ‘need’ to create, as if he were somehow lonely or in need of self-expression. The doctrine of the Trinity reminds us that an ‘Other’ already existed in himself. God as Trinity already was a community of love. God chose to share that community of love with his creation that he called into being. Creation is a gracious gift to his creatures – God was not pressured to create by reasons outside of himself (Eph 1:11; Rev 4:11).

fromNothingToSomethingWellOrdered.body:
God’s creation is structured and orderly. He brings distinction and separation: day from night, light from darkness, etc. This gives an underpinning for science. If creation was random, there would be no sense in looking for order within the randomness. Many of the leaders of the scientific revolution in sixteenth- and seventeenth-century Europe were Christians.[[fn:11]] Partly because they were Christians, and believed in a God of order who had created an ordered universe, they had the confidence needed to look for an underlying order within the (apparent) randomness of events in the world.[[fn:12]][[fn:13]]

God’s ordering of creation is true physically, and also morally. Our world has moral order built into it, waiting to be discerned. This does not make moral order a rival to God, because the moral order that God has created is an expression of his character. In other words, the doctrine of creation’s orderliness – its God-given structure – denies two distinct alternatives:

- **Creation is not chaotic**. It is not random, or purposeless, or meaningless. God has given it a structure and the more we study creation – in all its facets (from physics to psychology, from mathematics to the mating rituals of mosquitoes), at all its levels (from astrophysics to sub-atomic particles) – the more we can expect to discover that order.

- **Creation is not a blank canvas**. In the next chapter we will think more about humanity’s ‘sub-creative’ role within God’s purposes. God has left room for us to shape the world around us. But that world already comes with its own structure and order and integrity. The question is whether we will work creatively with the grain of the universe, or whether we will try to fight against that grain. The point here is that creation is not a blank canvas for us to shape in any way we so choose; rather it comes with existing structure that we are to respect.

Oliver O’Donovan puts this well:

Christians should confess their faith in the natural order as the good creation of God. To do this is to acknowledge that there are limits to the employment of technique and limits to the appropriateness of our ‘making.’ These limits will not be taught us by compassion, but only by the understanding of what God has made, and by a discovery that it is complete, whole, and satisfying.[[fn:14]]

God intends us to ‘make’ and be creative – but within the limits of the creation he has already established. When we do this we will find satisfaction in his good gifts to us; when we over-reach ourselves we share again in the first sin of our original parents, Adam and Eve, and set ourselves up in disharmony with God and his creation. Volume 2, Chapter 18 goes into more detail on how we may discern this order in creation.

extrasTheEuthyphroDilemma.body:
Plato (and much of later philosophy) never understood that God’s created moral order was an expression of his character. Plato framed the issue as a dilemma:[[fn:15]]

(a) Is lying wrong because God says so?\
or\
(b) God tells us not to lie, because it’s already wrong?

If (a) is true, then that seems to imply that morality is arbitrary, and God could have decided otherwise; he could have decided to make a world where lying is right, and truth-telling is wrong – and we all would have been expected to embrace lying and reject truth-telling. (This seems ‘counter-intuitive.’)

If (b) is true, then it seems like God is conforming to a higher standard that already exists outside of his creative act – which seems to imply there is something outside of God, or greater than God after all.

All dilemmas of this sort turn out to be ‘false dilemmas’ or ‘false dichotomies.’ That means you are being asked to choose between two possibilities, as if those were the only two possibilities available – yet both of them are wrong, and the right answer is a third option that is not presented to you. In this case, the correct option is that morality *is* a standard that already exists before God begins creating the universe, namely his own character – it is *not* a ‘higher’ standard that is somehow ‘outside’ of him. The moral order he builds into creation reflects that character.

theIntelligibilityOfCreation.body: Often the created order is not immediately intelligible, at least not in terms of how it appears superficially. The vagaries of the weather, the inscrutability of why lightning should strike one tree and not another, the seeming randomness of why a pandemic should arise from one place in one year and not another in another year – all these things and many more do not seem immediately intelligible. The doctrine of creation gives us confidence to look for an intelligibility underneath the superficial unintelligibility. The universe was not created by a God of chaos, but a God of faithfulness, and order, and intelligibility. It was created by the Word of God. All the ‘laws of nature’ are dependent on the Word of God as their source.

creationAndTime.body: Consider the question: *Was the act of Creation an act in time?* This is not an easy question to answer – if ‘yes’ that seems to make time stand outside creation (as uncreated?); but if no, then that begs more questions of how time and creation fit together. The problem arises because the question is wrongly framed. With Augustine, it is better to think, not of God creating the world ‘in’ time, but of him creating the world ‘with’ time.[[fn:16]] In other words, time itself is part of God’s creation – which suggests that eternity, from ‘within’ which God creates the universe (including time) is something greater than and beyond time.

ongoingSustenance.body:
The Bible describes God as upholding the world (Heb 1:3; Col 1:17; Acts 17:25). The Hebrew participles used for God’s creative work also imply ongoing activity (cf. Job 9:8-9; Ps 104:2-3; Isa 42:5; 44:24; 45:18), though this is not always obvious in translation. Also, the Bible presents all of the following as works of God: maintaining the stars and seasons (Job 38:31-33; Isa 40:26; Acts 14:17); the weather (Job 38; Matt 5:45); animal life cycles (Job 39; Matt 6:28-30); human life cycles (Ps 104:27-29); and human skills (farming, Isa 28:24-25; metalwork, Isa 54:16; other crafts Exod 31:2-5; and warfare, Ps 144:1).[[fn:17]] Milne expresses this point well:

God has called the universe into being out of nothing, and hence at every moment it ‘hangs’ suspended, as it were, over the abyss of non-existence. If God were to withdraw his upholding Word, then all being, spiritual and material, would instantly tumble back into nothing and cease to exist. The continuation of the universe from one moment to the next is therefore as great a miracle, and as fully the work of God, as is its coming into being at the beginning. In this profound sense we all live every instant only by the grace of God; our every breath is his gift.[[fn:18]]

#### The *dangers* of the ‘God of the gaps’ approach

Sometimes Christians have tried to demonstrate God’s ongoing role in created order by pointing to areas where our understanding of the processes of creation are incomplete, where we can’t (fully) explain what happens and why in terms of the structure of creation itself. In previous centuries people might have pointed to the motion of the stars, or the complexity of the weather as places in created order where God’s ongoing handiwork can ‘still’ be seen; more recently people might point to the beginning of human life as a place where God’s handiwork can ‘still’ be seen. In this understanding, God is seen as being active in the ‘gaps’ in our scientific understanding of the world. The problem is not in seeing God as being active in those areas. The problem is in thinking he is *only* active in those areas, or *specially*, or *additionally* active there. This is wrong. God is actively sustaining, and sovereignly superintending all of his world: ‘Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? Yet not one of them will fall to the ground outside your Father’s care. And even the very hairs of your head are all numbered’ (Matt 10:29-30). God is sovereign over the processes we understand (to whatever degree, at a creaturely level), as well as being sovereign of the processes we do not understand (to any degree, at a creaturely level). Reducing God’s activity to only the gaps in our knowledge demonstrates a weak grasp of God’s sustenance of all things, all the time.

dependentIndependence.body:
The universe is ‘contingent’ not ‘necessary,’ in the sense that it did not have to exist – God was not required to create it (and he might have created it in a very different way from how he did). And yet, having been created by the faithful God, it is stable, reliable, and consistent, upheld by the purposes of covenant love, his faithful ongoing sustenance. When considered in themselves, created things are fleeting, changeable, and weak. But when considered in the light of the faithfulness of their Creator, we can have confidence in them being maintained by the sustaining power of the Word of God. By grace, he preserves them from falling back into non-existence. The universe is neither self-supporting, nor mere illusion. In creating the world *ex nihilo* God has freely brought it into being as something totally distinct from himself, and yet as something having its own reality and thus a measure of genuine independence. This produces a certain paradox: creation’s God-given independence is itself dependent upon God. ‘If God were to withdraw his creative life and power, all creation would disintegrate and perish.’[[fn:19]][[fn:20]]

#### Miracles

God is all-powerful, so he could work directly all the time if he wanted to. He could continually overrule the normal processes of created order, and could cause miracles to happen non-stop. God could feed the widow and the orphan by making food spring into being every time they get out their plates. But God does not do this. Only rarely[[fn:21]] does God do anything like this. The reason for this is that God is the Creator. He has *created* creation. He has created it to work in a particular way, and he wants it to work that way, and he likes it to work that way. Of course, the Fall (see Chapter 4) has spoiled God’s good purposes in creation. God is certainly acting to overcome how his creation has been spoiled. But he overcomes it by redeeming creation, not by overthrowing it or overriding it. God does not normally overthrow the workings of created order, even for the important, laudable, and life-sustaining task of feeding orphans and widows. This tells us that:

1. Created order is tremendously important to God. It is so important to him that he delights to work *through* created means, rather than around them. God delights to feed orphans and widows by sanctifying the communities they live in, so that he feeds them through moral growth of those around them, rather than bypassing those communities to feed them miraculously and directly.

2. When miracles do happen, they are generally signalling that something *massively* important is happening in God’s purposes for the world – and so we should pay attention.[[fn:22]]

This does not explain why a particular person goes hungry, and it never excuses us from feeding them: the call to feed the hungry is a call to act, not to wait for a miracle.

aNoteAboutTheLanguageOfNature.header: A note about the language of ‘Nature’
aNoteAboutTheLanguageOfNature.body: In English it is common to speak about ‘nature’ as well as ‘creation’ – in some circles the language of ‘nature’ may be much more common than ‘creation.’ There is nothing wrong with any word, so long as we know what it means. But ‘nature’, in the sense of an independent physical power, is not a category the Bible itself uses, and so we have to find a definition outside of Scripture – and the definition(s) people choose may not always be consistent with Scripture. Often people use it to mean something like ‘the creative and regulative physical power which is conceived of as operating in the physical world and as the immediate cause of all its phenomena.’[[fn:23]] Such definitions can cause trouble, as ‘nature’ then becomes a rival or alternative to God. I would suggest that you are more likely to remain faithful in your theological thinking if you train yourself to think of ‘creation’ or ‘the created order’ as your primary terminology, and leave ‘nature’ as a derivative (and slightly slippery!) term that you will have to keep an eye on, and keep redefining in terms of your understanding of creation.

creationsPurposeGodsGlory.body:
All of creation glorifies God (Ps 19:1), but in different ways. Erickson draws out how obedience brings glory to God: ‘inanimate creation does so mechanically, obeying natural laws that govern the physical world. The animate creation does so instinctively, responding to impulses within. Only humans and angels are capable of obeying God consciously and willingly and thus glorifying God most fully.’[[fn:24]] Creation also glorifies God through its own, modest glory, since he is the one who created that creaturely glory. Creation’s glory, in this sense, includes a whole range of characteristics, for example:[[fn:25]]

- **Beauty**. Creation is filled with beauty: the colours of a sunset; the delicacy of a flower; the wonder of a nebula. And God’s beauty surpasses all of this.

- **Complexity**. From the miracles of DNA to the intricacies of quantum mechanics, creation can be mind-bogglingly complex to understand; yet is simplicity itself to the mind of its Creator.

- **Hugeness** (both physical and temporal). A rocket, travelling at 1000km/s (that’s about 2.2 million mph) would take about 1,300 years to travel from earth to Proxima Centauri, our nearest star. It would take about 30 million years to travel all the way across the galaxy, and about 28 trillion years to travel across the observable universe. And yet these distances and timescales are vanishingly small before our infinite God.[[fn:26]]

- **Goodness**. The goodness of creation, and the joy it brings us, point to the goodness of the ultimate Joy-giver, who created it all and pronounced it ‘very good.’

Creation’s ‘glory’ points beyond itself to God’s greater glory.

thePlaceOfTheFatherSonAndSpirit.header: The Place of the Father, Son, and Spirit
thePlaceOfTheFatherSonAndSpirit.body: God, as Father, Son, and Spirit, is totally unique – he alone is the Creator, he alone is worthy of our worship and adoration. Creation is ontologically distinct from its Creator. And God has total authority over creation: he made it, so he owns it, so he decides the rules. A strong doctrine of creation also keeps us from downgrading Christ’s incarnation. Suppose for a moment that the physical world was somehow inherently evil; then it would be almost impossible to accept that the Son – the Second Person of the Trinity! – could take on a physical (and therefore evil!) human body. By contrast, correctly understanding that God’s creation is good means that the incarnation makes sense.[[fn:27]]

thePlaceOfHumanity.body:
The next chapter concentrates on humanity’s place within creation, but we include a short summary here:

- **Image of God**. Humanity has been made in the image of God, and so occupies a special, privileged, and precious place within creation. And also a place of great responsibility.

- **Relationship**. Humanity has been made for relationship: relationship with God, with one another, and with the rest of creation.

- **Reigning**. Humanity has been given the task of reigning over God’s creation under him. However, that reign should be according to the pattern of God’s reign – which is a pattern of care, not domination. We are granted stewardship under God, not independent ownership.

thePlaceOfSpiritualPowers.body: This topic is treated more fully in Chapter 6. For now, we note that whatever spiritual powers there exist, they are creaturely powers, not divine powers. They are servants of God – either faithful servants carrying out his will, or else rebellious servants whose powers are limited, and whose days of rebellion are numbered.

thePlaceOfTheRestOfCreation.header: The Place of the rest of Creation
thePlaceOfTheRestOfCreation.body: Creation is intended to bring glory to God. It is the product of his productive work, entrusted to humanity to steward. The whole of creation is metaphorically pictured as longing for God’s purposes to be fulfilled (cf. Rom 8:19-21), and as rejoicing when those purposes will be fulfilled (cf. Ps 96:11-13).

worshipAndPraise.body: Creation – in all its beautiful and wonderful complexity – gives us unending reasons to praise our Creator. ‘You are worthy, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honour and power, for you created all things, and by your will they were created and have their being’ (Rev 4:11).

orderVsBlankCanvas.body: The fact that we live in an ordered creation – which includes a moral ordering – has profound implications for morality and ethics, for issues of life and death, sex, parenthood, reproduction, and medicine. A solidly Christian approach to ethics, including bioethics, depends upon a substantive doctrine of created moral order. We will consider these issues in more detail in the next chapter, and in Volume 2 (especially Chapters 12, 13 and 18).

theEnvironmentEcologyAndSustainability.body:
God has an eye to the well-being of even the birds of the air and the grass of the field (Matt 6:26-30; 10:29). Everything has value and deserves respect since it is *God’s* creation. There is a sense in which it is ‘ours’ too: it is ours to steward – and stewardship should have respect built in. Respect, however, should not entail worship. As Erickson notes: ‘Only God deserves our worship. Everything else exists for his sake, not he for its sake. Although we will highly respect the creation, since it has been made by him, we will always maintain a clear distinction between God and it.’[[fn:28]] Calvin B. DeWitt argues for four ecological principles arising from the doctrine of creation. McGrath[[fn:29]] summarises DeWitt’s principles as:

1. **The ‘earth-keeping principle’**: just as the creator keeps and sustains humanity, so humanity must keep and sustain the creator’s creation.

2. **The ‘sabbath principle’**: the creation must be allowed to recover from human use of its resources.

3. **The ‘fruitfulness principle’**: the fecundity of the creation is to be enjoyed, not destroyed.

4. **The ‘fulfillment and limits principle’**: there are limits set to humanity’s role within creation, with boundaries set in place which must be respected.[[fn:30]]

Volume 2, Chapter 23 develops a fuller theology of ecology and the environment, including the Sabbath rest of the land.

thinkingAboutEvil.body:
We cannot excuse our evil behaviour by blaming the evil realm of the physical world – because it is not inherently evil! Nor can we blame society (as if individuals are basically OK, and it is only wider society that leads them into sin) – because human society is also not inherently evil. It is part of the good world God originally made.[[fn:31]] McGrath summarises Augustine’s view of creation, and its relation to evil, as follows:

1. Everything that exists owes that existence to God. There is no alternative source or origin of existence.

2. Everything that exists was created good by a good God.

3. The evil that exists within the world is not to be thought of as something positive and real, possessing its own distinct substance. Rather, it is to be thought of as a ‘lack of goodness.’

4. Evil does not derive its origin from God but from humanity’s use of its God-given freedom.[[fn:32]]

We will give further consideration to the ‘problem’ of evil in Chapter 5.

freedomToEnjoyGodsGiftsInCreation.header: Freedom to Enjoy God’s Gifts in Creation
freedomToEnjoyGodsGiftsInCreation.body: A strong doctrine of creation provides a counterweight against asceticism. If you think the physical creation is in some way evil, you are likely to be suspicious of the human body, and physical pleasure. This has led some Christians to seek godliness in the realm of the ‘spiritual’ only, by emphasising ascetic spiritual disciplines (e.g. fasting, meditation, and/or solitude) and simultaneously arguing that the truly ‘spiritual’ will avoid sex and other physical pleasure (e.g. from a varied and pleasant diet).[[fn:33]] These disciplines are good in themselves; the mistake is to think that the physical is the problem.

aPostScriptOnChronology.body:
The attentive reader may have noticed that this chapter has not yet addressed the issue of the chronology of creation. Often lots of effort is spent on debating the chronology of creation (e.g. ‘six days’ vs ‘millions of years’). This issue is not without importance for our wider theology, but that importance is indirect – its importance comes from how it impacts our doctrine of Scripture, and our understanding of hermeneutics. To clarify this distinction between ‘direct’ and ‘indirect’ consequences, consider the following examples.

First, if we change our view on creation *ex nihilo* then direct theological consequences follow. If God created the universe out of some pre-existing matter that was not created by him, then it follows directly that God is not the only eternal being – either the pre-existing matter is also eternal, or whatever created it (whether a single entity, or an ongoing chain of them) is eternal. Either way, our understanding of God’s nature is immediately and fundamentally changed. And, in addition, there may be secondary, indirect consequences for our doctrine of Scripture, and/or our understanding of hermeneutics.

Second, if we change our view on the chronology of creation – suppose we change our view from a ‘six day creation’ to a ‘three day creation,’ or perhaps we change our view of the age of the earth from a billion years old to a trillion years old – then no direct theological consequences follow. Nothing in the rest of theology hangs directly on whether creation took three days, or six days (or three billion years, or six trillion years). There may, however, be secondary, indirect consequences for our doctrine of Scripture, and/or our understanding of hermeneutics.

It is not wrong to pay attention to the chronology of creation; but sometimes so much attention gets paid to this that we forget to concentrate on the actual theology of creation(!) – the doctrines that have direct consequences as well as indirect ones – such as the kind of matters discussed in this chapter and the next. Therefore, in this chapter I have attempted to redress the balance by giving priority to the *doctrine* of creation. A number of excellent – and detailed – treatments of the chronology of creation are available, and the interested reader is referred to these: for an extensive, but even-handed overview, which concludes that both ‘young earth’ and ‘old earth’ views are possible, see Wayne Grudem;[[fn:34]] for an ‘old earth, but non-theistic-evolution view’ see Erickson;[[fn:35]] for a more sympathetic approach to theistic evolution see McGrath.[[fn:36]]

summary.body:
1\. God alone is eternal. He created everything else by his word, out of nothing, and without conflict or violence. He is the sole Creator, and the only one worthy of worship.

2\. Creation is distinct from God, yet depends on him at every moment. Against deism, God is not distant; against pantheism, the world is not God. God is both transcendent and immanent.

3\. Against dualism and gnosticism, creation is good – ‘very good’ is the Bible’s own verdict – and God has no rival. Evil is not part of the original creation – and since there was a time when evil entered creation, we can hope for a time when it is evicted.

4\. Creation is ordered and intelligible, and it has a real integrity of its own. God sustains it, and normally works through created means.

5\. Creation has a built-in order, including a moral order, which expresses God’s character rather than being either an arbitrary rule or a standard above him. Our own creativity is meant to flourish within the bounds that God’s creation sets.

6\. Creation exists for God’s glory. Father, Son, and Spirit each have a part in it, and spiritual powers, however real, are creatures, not rivals to God.

7\. We are called to steward creation – not to own it, and not to worship it – and to enjoy it as God’s gift. This shapes how we think about evil, our bodies, and the environment.

toolsMyself.header: Tools for Making Disciples: For myself
toolsMyself.body:
The doctrine of creation is meant to shape how we live, not only what we believe. These prompts take it in three directions: towards myself, towards someone I am helping, and towards our church. Use the ones that fit.

- Do I treat my body, my work, or my possessions as something to escape, to worship, or to own – rather than to steward?

- Do I suspect that enjoying food, rest, or beauty is somehow less spiritual than prayer? Where did that idea come from?

- Which gift of creation – a meal, a view, a night’s sleep – can I receive this week with thanks to the Creator?

- What one everyday practice – eating, resting, working, throwing things away – will I change this month because everything I use is God’s creation?

toolsSomeoneElse.header: Tools for Making Disciples: For someone I am helping
toolsSomeoneElse.body:
Begin by listening to the person’s story and reasons; these prompts are for opening a conversation, not for diagnosing someone from a distance. Try to understand where someone’s view of the material world might have drifted towards escaping it, worshipping it, or ignoring it – rather than stewarding it.

- Do they treat the physical world – body, work, possessions – as something to escape, or as something to steward?

- Do they attribute too much meaning to nature (worship), or too little (dismissal)?

- Where might they be acting as an owner rather than as a steward?

- Can they name one everyday practice – eating, resting, working, throwing things away – that their doctrine of creation should change?

toolsChurch.header: Tools for Making Disciples: For our church
toolsChurch.body:
- Do our prayers and songs thank God for creation – food, rain, bodies, seasons – as well as for salvation?

- How do we treat our land, buildings, water, and rubbish? Would a visitor see that we believe they belong to God?

- Do we teach that the body and its pleasures are good gifts within God’s order, or do we leave people suspecting that the physical is second-rate?

- When we explain why things go wrong – sickness, poverty, conflict – do we blame the world itself, or do we speak honestly of sin while still calling creation good?

naomiRevisited.body:
It would be easy to try to argue Naomi out of her experience, as though the aim were to make her feel less connected to the world around her. That would be a mistake. Naomi is half right, and it is worth telling her so.

Genesis agrees with her that the world is full of meaning and worthy of wonder – but as a gift, not as God himself. Pantheism, the view Naomi is drifting towards, dissolves the difference between Creator and creation until there is no one left to thank. Christianity keeps that difference, and in keeping it, keeps room for a real relationship. Nor is the God of Genesis cold: he looks at all he has made and calls it ‘very good.’

Naomi is not a drop merging into an ocean, but a creature known and addressed by the God who made the ocean. Her sense of belonging to something bigger than herself can become a pointer to the Creator she was made to know (Rom 1:20).

questionsForReflection.body:
1\. Where in your own thinking do you notice traces of deism (God distant and uninvolved) or pantheism (God and the world blurred together)?

2\. The chapter notes that in Genesis the cosmos is created ‘through peaceful speech not the carnage of war.’ How should that shape a Christian response to conflict and chaos?

3\. What does it mean, in practice, to be a steward rather than an owner of creation? Choose one area of your life – money, the environment, your body – and apply it.

4\. How should the doctrine of creation affect the way you worship God, think about evil, treat animals, and throw away rubbish? Pick two or three of these and note the connections.

technicalTerms.body:
Deism: Belief that God created the world, but has now withdrawn from it.

Demiurge: Used by the Gnostics for their lesser, evil god who they thought had created the universe.

Dualism: Belief in: ‘**Two** equal and opposite powers of good and evil’

Epistemology: The study of how we *know* things (often contrasted with ontology).

*Ex nihilo*: Creation ‘out of nothing’

Gnosticism: Heresy that emphasised spiritual knowledge and viewed physical existence as evil.

Immanence: God being and acting within the universe, in communion with the world that he has created, continuously sustaining it.

Ontology: The study of the *nature* or *being* of things (often contrasted with epistemology).

Panentheism: Belief that the world exists within God, while God is also more than the world.

Pantheism: Belief that God is everything, and everything is God.

Transcendence: God being above and beyond creation, wholly other to creation, wholly distinct from it.

furtherReading.body:
### Key Bible Passages

Gen 1-2; Job 38-42; Ps 8:1-9; 19:1-6; 24:1-2; 33:6-9; 104; John 1:1-14; 1 Cor 8:6; Col 1:16-17; Heb 1:10.

**Berkhof, Louis. *Systematic Theology*.** Edinburgh: Banner of Truth, 1958.\
A long-standing Reformed textbook, concise and orderly; cited here on the original creation and the New Creation. Older in style; for students and pastors.

**Erickson, Millard J. *Christian Theology*.** 3rd ed. Grand Rapids, MI: Baker Academic, 2013.\
A full, readable evangelical systematic theology, used throughout this chapter, including for an ‘old earth’ view of the chronology of creation. For students, pastors, and serious lay readers.

**Grudem, Wayne. *Systematic Theology: An Introduction to Biblical Doctrine*.** Grand Rapids, MI: Zondervan, 1994.\
A full evangelical systematic theology; chapter 15 sets out the main views on the age of the earth fairly before giving its own tentative conclusion. For students and pastors.

**Hamilton, Janet, Bernard Hamilton, and Yuri Stoyanov. *Christian Dualist Heresies in the Byzantine World, c. 650-c. 1450: Selected Sources*.** Manchester: Manchester University Press, 1998.\
Translated primary sources on the dualist movements of the Byzantine world.\
Specialist; for readers who want to see what dualism looked like in practice.

**Harrison, Peter. *The Bible, Protestantism, and the Rise of Natural Science***. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998.\
A scholarly study of how Protestant ways of reading the Bible helped shape early modern natural science. For students.

**Mangalwadi, Vishal. *The Book That Made Your World: How the Bible Created the Soul of Western Civilization*.** Nashville, TN: Thomas Nelson, 2011.\
A popular, wide-ranging account of how the Bible has shaped the modern West, including its science. Accessible; for all readers.

**McGrath, Alister E. *A Scientific Theology*. Vol. 1, *Nature*.** Edinburgh: T&T Clark; Grand Rapids, MI: Eerdmans, 2001.\
A rigorous work on how theology and the natural sciences relate; cited here on the language of ‘nature.’ Demanding; for advanced students.

**McGrath, Alister E. *Christian Theology: An Introduction*.** 6th ed. Chichester: Wiley Blackwell, 2017.\
A clear introduction to the whole of Christian doctrine, cited here on Augustine and evil and on ecology (ch. 9). A good first read for students and lay readers.

**Milne, Bruce. *Know the Truth: A Handbook of Christian Belief*.** 3rd ed. Nottingham: IVP, 2009.\
An accessible evangelical handbook, and this chapter’s main source on God’s upholding of the world. For all readers.

**O’Donovan, Oliver. *Begotten or Made?*** Oxford: Clarendon, 1984.\
A short book on the limits of human ‘making’ and the givenness of created order.\
Concise but demanding; for students and pastors willing to read slowly.

**Reed, Rodney L., and David K. Ngaruiya, eds. *God and Creation*.** Africa Society of Evangelical Theology Series. Carlisle: Langham Global Library, 2019.\
Essays from African perspectives on God as Creator, creation care and the environment, and human relationships; for pastors, students, and serious lay readers.

**Thiselton, Anthony C. ‘Creation.’ In *The Thiselton Companion to Christian Theology*.** Grand Rapids, MI: Eerdmans, 2015.\
A short entry, useful on the shape of Genesis 1 (non-order rather than chaos). For students and pastors.

**Torrance, Thomas F. *The Trinitarian Faith: The Evangelical Theology of the Ancient Catholic Church*.** 2nd ed. London: T&T Clark, 1997.\
A demanding account of the Nicene faith; its treatment of creation lies behind ‘Dependent Independence’ (ch. 3, pp. 76-109). For advanced students.

**Watkin, Christopher. *Biblical Critical Theory: How the Bible’s Unfolding Story Makes Sense of Modern Life and Culture*.** Grand Rapids, MI: Zondervan, 2022.\
A long, readable book that reads modern culture through the Bible’s story; ch. 2, cited here, bears on the violence of other origin stories. For pastors and serious lay readers.
